costGuide.labourLine: Fitting a Nissan K9K typically takes 6-9 hours at an independent specialist rate of £65/hr, resulting in a typical fitted premium of £390-£585 . Confirm exact labour when comparing quotes.
paragraphs: The final cost of a K9K replacement is heavily influenced by the condition of the fuel injectors and turbocharger, which are the two most common wear items on high-mileage 1.5 dCi units. A proper reconditioned K9K will include new or refurbished injectors, a cleaned or replaced DPF, and updated turbo seals. Always verify that the EGR system has been addressed, as carbon buildup is a primary driver of replacement demand. failures.title: Nissan K9K Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Injector Failure (Swarf Contamination & Electrical Faults) - 2005-2018 units
items.whatHappens: The K9K's piezoelectric injectors are susceptible to wear, electrical faults, and contamination from metallic swarf in the fuel system. Symptoms include rough idling, excessive black smoke, difficulty starting, and a noticeable loss of power. If an injector leaks, it can wash down the cylinder walls, diluting the engine oil and leading to rapid bearing wear.
items.repairVsReplace: While a single faulty injector can be replaced, it is common for multiple injectors to fail in sequence on high-mileage units. If oil dilution has occurred, a full engine replacement is often the most reliable and cost-effective long-term solution. Read our full injector failure guide.

items.title: Turbocharger Failure and Overfuelling - 2005-2018 units
items.whatHappens: The K9K turbocharger relies on a precise, clean oil supply. If the engine has been run low on oil (sometimes masked by earlier injector leak diluting the sump), the turbo bearings can fail. This leads to blue exhaust smoke, significant loss of power, and metallic rattling from the turbine housing. Overfuelling from a stuck injector can also over-speed and destroy the turbo.
items.repairVsReplace: A failing turbo can sometimes be replaced independently. However, if oil starvation or swarf contamination has occurred, debris may have circulated through the K9K oil galleries, necessitating a full unit replacement to prevent immediate secondary failure of the new turbo. Read our full turbocharger failure guide.

items.title: EGR Clogging and DPF Blockage
items.whatHappens: As a compact diesel frequently used in urban environments, the K9K is prone to EGR valve clogging and Diesel Particulate Filter (DPF) blockage. This prevents proper exhaust flow, triggering engine management lights and forcing the vehicle into "limp mode".
items.repairVsReplace: A DPF clean or EGR service can provide temporary relief. However, if the clogging has caused excessive backpressure, it can lead to turbocharger failure, necessitating a full unit replacement. Read our full DPF failure guide.

failures.goodYearsLine: Later revisions of the K9K family (such as the 844 and 846 variants) feature improved injector seals and more robust turbo actuators, significantly reducing the incidence of these failures .

variants.title: K9K Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: INTRO: The K9K 1.5 dCi is a massive family of engines. While they share the same core 1.5L block, they differ by power output, emission standard (Euro 4/5/6), and specific vehicle calibration. Identifying your exact sub-code is critical when sourcing a replacement. - Fitted to: Early Nissan Qashqai J10. - Key technical difference: Pre-DPF or early DPF application, simpler turbo actuator. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family injector and turbo failure pattern. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with later Euro 5/6 variants due to ECU mapping and DPF plumbing differences. - Fitted to: Nissan Juke F15, later Qashqai J10/J11. - Key technical difference: Higher output calibration, mandatory DPF fitment. - Sub-code-specific failure note: DPF clogging is more prevalent due to urban Juke usage patterns. - Interchange note: Requires matching DPF and ECU software; loom connectors may differ from 830. - Fitted to: Nissan Note E11/E12, lower-spec Qashqai. - Key technical difference: Lower boost pressure, smaller turbocharger. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above. - Interchange note: Physically interchangeable with 832 in some cases, but will trigger ECU limp mode without remapping. - Fitted to: Late-model Qashqai J11, Juke F15 facelift. - Key technical difference: Revised injector seals, updated turbo actuator, AdBlue/SCR integration on some applications. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Significantly more robust; injector and turbo failures are far less reported after these revisions.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement K9K - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used K9K is only advisable for budget-conscious owners of low-value host vehicles, provided the unit comes with a verifiable service history and no history of DPF-related limp mode or injector failure. Given the commercial and urban nature of many host vehicles, mileage verification is critical to avoid inheriting a unit near the end of its service life. Explore used Nissan engines.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned K9K is the most recommended path for most owners. A reputable rebuild will address the core weaknesses by fitting new or refurbished piezoelectric injectors, cleaning or replacing the DPF, and renewing all turbocharger seals and EGR components. This resolves the dominant failure patterns while keeping costs well below a full custom rebuild. Explore reconditioned Nissan engines.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified if the original K9K suffered catastrophic failure due to severe oil dilution from a leaking injector or a seized turbocharger sending metallic debris into the oil galleries. An upgraded rebuild should include new pistons, a machined block, and an updated oil pump to prevent future lubrication issues. Explore rebuilt Nissan engines.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Our network of vetted UK specialists can supply the K9K unit and handle the complete installation, including ECU adaptation and DPF regeneration cycles, backed by a minimum 12-month warranty. Learn more about supply & fit.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The K9K is typically found in Nissan Qashqai, Juke, and Note models valued between £1,000 and £10,000 depending on age, mileage, and specification. If your vehicle is at the lower end of this spectrum (e.g., an early 2006-2010 Nissan Note E11 valued under £2,000), a £1,500+ reconditioned engine replacement may exceed 75% of the car's current market value, triggering a 🔴 Scrap Threshold warning. In these specific scenarios, it is financially prudent to evaluate the vehicle's scrap or part-exchange value first. However, for well-maintained, higher-value Qashqai and Juke examples, investing in a properly reconditioned K9K remains a cost-effective alternative to vehicle replacement.

items.question: What is the most common problem with the Nissan K9K 1.5 dCi?
items.answer: The dominant failures are piezoelectric injector wear (often with swarf contamination) and turbocharger failure, typically emerging between 80,000 and 150,000 miles. Symptoms include rough idling, excessive black smoke, and limp mode from restricted exhaust flow or overfuelling. Ignoring injector leaks leads to oil dilution and catastrophic bearing failure.

items.answer: The K9K 1.5L dCi was fitted to the Nissan Qashqai (J10/J11), Juke (F15), and Note (E11/E12) from 2005 to 2018. It serves as the primary compact diesel workhorse across these models. Always verify your specific chassis via registration lookup before ordering.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned K9K engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned K9K is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the high risk of latent injector and DPF failures in high-mileage urban vehicles. A proper recon includes refurbished injectors, a cleaned or replaced DPF, and renewed turbo seals. A used unit may simply pass the same downtime risk to your car.

items.question: How do I know if my car has the K9K engine code?
items.answer: The K9K code (and its specific sub-code, e.g., 832 or 844) is stamped on a machined pad on the engine block and is listed on your V5C document. It is frequently confused with the larger 1.6 dCi (R9M) or older 1.9 dCi (F9Q). Fitting the wrong revision causes ECU mapping conflicts and emissions system incompatibility.
